passages.happening:
The Spirit brings Ezekiel to the east gate, where twenty-five men stand, among them ‘Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, who were leaders of the people’ (verse 1). They plot evil and say, ‘Is not the time near to build houses? The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat’ (verse 3).

God answers that the only meat in the pot is the people they have killed in the city (verses 6-7). He will bring them out of the city and judge them at the borders of Israel (verses 9-11). As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah dies. Ezekiel falls on his face and cries, ‘Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
A cooking pot protects the meat inside from the fire. The leaders meant that Jerusalem's walls would protect them and that they were the prime cut of the nation, while the exiles were the scraps thrown away. Their saying about building houses showed confidence that life would go on as normal. God turns their picture around.

These two leaders are otherwise unknown; this Jaazaniah is not the son of Shaphan in chapter 8. The text does not say whether Pelatiah's death also happened at that moment in Jerusalem, and interpreters differ.
passages.later: Jeremiah said the exiles were the good figs: ‘Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah’ (Jeremiah 24:5). Jerusalem's leaders who stayed were the bad figs (Jeremiah 24:8).
passages.hard:
Did Pelatiah really die because of Ezekiel's prophecy, and why would God strike him down?

The text reports that Pelatiah died while Ezekiel was prophesying in his vision. Some take it as something Ezekiel later learned had really happened in Jerusalem, a confirmation that his visions were true. Others think the death belongs within the vision, a sign of what was coming for the leaders. The text does not settle it.

What it makes clear is Ezekiel's reaction: not satisfaction but alarm. His cry leads straight to God's answer, that a remnant will be gathered and given a new heart.
passages.asks: The leaders thought they were the best of the nation and the exiles were scraps. Ask whom you are tempted to look down on as far from God. And ask whether God might be closer to them than you think.

passages.t: A sanctuary for the exiles, and a new heart
passages.happening:
The people of Jerusalem said of the exiles, ‘They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession’ (verse 15). God answers, ‘yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone’ (verse 16). He will gather them and give them back the land, and they will remove its idols (verses 17-18).

‘And I will give them singleness of heart and put a new spirit within them; I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh’ (verse 19), so that they will keep his ways. ‘Then they will be My people, and I will be their God’ (verse 20).

Then the cherubim rise, ‘And the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city and stood over the mountain east of the city’ (verse 23). The Spirit carries Ezekiel back to the exiles, and he tells them everything (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
After 597 BC, those left in Jerusalem seem to have told themselves that they were the true Israel and the exiles had lost their share in the land. Property left by deported families may have passed into their hands.

God's answer is stunning. The exiles, who had no temple, had God himself as their sanctuary. The word for relatives in verse 15 comes from the Hebrew for a redeemer, the close relative responsible for buying back lost land.

A heart of stone is hard and unresponsive; a heart of flesh is alive and able to hear. The mountain east of the city is the Mount of Olives. The glory has now left the city entirely.
passages.later: Jeremiah heard the same promise: ‘I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts’ (Jeremiah 31:33). Moses prayed, ‘Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations’ (Psalm 90:1).
passages.asks: God was a sanctuary for people who had lost their temple. Ask what you have lost that made you feel far from God. And ask what it would mean for him to be your sanctuary there.
